deep.reconstruction:
This page is the plate Tab. VII of E260 (Novi Commentarii Petropolitani VI). It contains only figures and labels, no text. The figures illustrate the paper's problems on outflow from a reservoir through pipes when wall friction is taken into account.

Fig. 1: a vessel AA–BB drains through a long vertical pipe BB–CC, issuing at the orifice CC.

Fig. 2: the same arrangement with dotted curves. One runs from β to B and shows the stream converging into the pipe entrance. The other runs from C to γ, where the pipe changes section. The outlet is DD.

Fig. 3: a horizontal pipe BB–CC discharging laterally at CC. The marks cc near the outlet appear to mark an element of the pipe.

Fig. 4: an inclined pipe from B down to CC. A dotted line carries the reservoir level AA horizontally to F, and a vertical line drops from F to C. FC is therefore the total head available at the outlet.

Fig. 5: a fountain. The inclined pipe B–E is fed from the reservoir, and a vertical nozzle DD at its end throws a jet up to G. G stays below the reservoir level line A–F, and the shortfall is the head lost to friction. A dotted alternative conduit b–b–c–c (down vertically, then horizontally to the nozzle) is drawn for comparison. It shows that a longer or differently routed pipe changes the frictional loss, and hence the jet height.

In modern terms, Euler adds a resistance term to the one-dimensional (hydraulic) Bernoulli/momentum balance for pipe flow. The term is proportional to the wetted perimeter times the length, divided by the cross-section, and grows with the square of the velocity. This is essentially a Chézy/Darcy-type head-loss law. He applies it to:
- steady and unsteady outflow,
- vertical, horizontal and inclined pipes,
- jet heights of fountains,
the last being the practical motivation (fountain design).
errors: None detectable: the page is a figure plate. The qualitative content (jet G below reservoir level F because of friction) is physically correct.

ideas.what: Head loss from wall friction in pipe flow, proportional to length × perimeter/area × v², reducing outlet velocity and fountain jet height below the reservoir level
ideas.modern_name: Darcy–Weisbach / Chézy pipe-friction head loss in the extended Bernoulli equation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Chézy (1770s), Prony, Darcy (1857), Weisbach (1845); Euler's E260 is noted as an early attempt
ideas.where_published: E260 itself, Novi Comm. Petrop. 6 (1761); discussed in the Opera omnia II.13 introduction (Truesdell)

ideas.what: Comparison of pipe routings (dotted conduit bbcc vs. inclined pipe) for the same fountain
ideas.modern_name: Dependence of head loss on pipe length/route in network design
ideas.where_published: E260 text; related to Euler's Sanssouci fountain work (E206 etc.)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a plate of figures belonging to a known, published paper whose content (Euler's pipe-friction theory) is discussed in the standard histories. There is nothing new on the page itself.
transcription_corrections: Fig. 2: the label read as '6' at the top right is the Greek β; γ is placed where the pipe narrows below C; the outlet is labelled D D.

Fig. 5: the labels are 'b' and 'bB' at the junction (a lowercase b beside the main B), and lowercase 'c' at the corners of the dotted conduit; 'c c' and 'E' are at the horizontal end piece; 'G' is the top of the jet.
